definition.text: Mathis Wackernagel is a Swiss-born sustainability advocate who co-created the ecological footprint and heads the Global Footprint Network.

facts.text: The ecological footprint concept and calculation method was his PhD work with supervisor William Rees at the University of British Columbia, from 1990 to 1994.
Footprint and biocapacity accounts compare human demand on nature with what nature can supply, and Global Footprint Network has developed them further since 2003.
He holds that climate change, biodiversity loss and food shortage are symptoms of one theme: humanity's use of resources has grown large compared with what Earth can renew.
With Rees he proposed that cost savings from efficiency gains be taxed away so they cannot cause a rebound in use.

definition.text: Milner Baily Schaefer (1912–1970) was an American fisheries scientist notable for his work on the population dynamics of fisheries.

facts.text: At the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission he published a fishery equilibrium model based on the Verhulst growth model, with a catch equation known as the Schaefer short-term catch equation.
He extended the model to an unregulated fishery where effort rises until no profit is left, the equilibrium H. Scott Gordon called bionomic equilibrium.
Together, Schaefer's and Gordon's work, now the Gordon–Schaefer model, laid the basis for quantitative fisheries economics.

title: Rachel Carson

definition.text: Rachel Carson (1907–1964) was an American marine biologist, writer and conservationist whose book Silent Spring (1962) is credited with advancing the global environmental movement.

facts.text: Silent Spring described the harmful effects of pesticides on the environment and helped focus opposition to DDT.
She argued pesticides are better called biocides because their effects rarely stay limited to the target pests.
One scholar wrote that after Silent Spring no one could easily sell pollution as the necessary underside of progress.
